overview.title: Loading arrays, splitting, and the encoder-decoder model
overview.section: 11.2 Training a segmentation model from scratch
overview.subsection: 11.2.2 Building and training the segmentation model
overview.main_topic: Filling the input/target arrays, holding out 1,000 validation samples, and defining a segmentation ConvNet of strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers
overview.central_idea: All images go into a float32 array of shape (num_imgs, 200, 200, 3) and all masks into a uint8 array of shape (num_imgs, 200, 200, 1); the last 1,000 become validation data. The model rescales pixels to [0, 1], compresses them with six Conv2D layers (three with stride 2) and expands them back with six Conv2DTranspose layers (three with stride 2), all with padding="same".
overview.importance: This is the first full segmentation architecture in the book: a symmetric downsample/upsample stack whose output keeps the input's spatial size, which is the structural requirement for per-pixel prediction.
learning_objectives: Explain the shapes and dtypes of input_imgs and targets
Perform a hold-out split with negative slicing
Trace the spatial size through every layer of get_model
Explain why padding="same" and Rescaling(1/255) are used

summary:
The page finishes the data preparation and starts the model.

**Loading.** The first block allocates `input_imgs = np.zeros((num_imgs,) + img_size + (3,), dtype="float32")` and `targets = np.zeros((num_imgs,) + img_size + (1,), dtype="uint8")`, i.e. shapes `(num_imgs, 200, 200, 3)` and `(num_imgs, 200, 200, 1)`, then loops over all indices calling the two helpers from p.337. The callout stresses that images and masks are stored in the same order, that inputs have three RGB channels and that targets have one channel holding integer labels.

**Splitting.** "As always", the arrays are split: `num_val_samples = 1000` are reserved for validation; `[:-num_val_samples]` takes everything except the last 1,000 for training and `[-num_val_samples:]` takes the last 1,000. Because the paths were shuffled on p.337, this tail is a random sample.

**Model (section 11.2.2).** `get_model(img_size, num_classes)` builds a Functional model:

- `keras.Input(shape=img_size + (3,))` and `Rescaling(1.0 / 255)`. The callout says not to forget to rescale input images to the [0–1] range;
- an **encoder** of six `Conv2D` layers with 64, 64, 128, 128, 256 and 256 filters, 3 × 3 kernels and ReLU, where every other layer has `strides=2`: 200 → 100 → 50 → 25;
- a **decoder** of six `Conv2DTranspose` layers with 256, 256, 128, 128, 64 and 64 filters, where every other layer has `strides=2`: 25 → 50 → 100 → 200.

A callout explains that `padding="same"` is used everywhere *to avoid the influence of border padding on feature map size*. Without it, each 3 × 3 convolution would trim two pixels and the decoder would not land exactly on 200 × 200. The final softmax layer and `keras.Model(...)` call are on p.339, where the authors also explain why strides replace max pooling and what `Conv2DTranspose` does.

paragraphs.excerpt: As always, let’s split the arrays into a training and a validation set:
paragraphs.what_it_says: The arrays are split into training and validation sets, with 1,000 samples reserved for validation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Simple hold-out validation (chapter 5's approach): the last 1,000 shuffled samples are never trained on and are used to monitor generalization and choose the best epoch (p.341).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Segmentation models overfit too (p.341 reports overfitting around epoch 25); without a validation set you could not detect it or checkpoint the best model.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Negative slicing: a[:-k] is all but the last k elements, a[-k:] is the last k elements; together they partition the array.

terminology.meaning: Reserving a fixed subset of the data for evaluation during development.

connections: p.337: shuffling makes the tail a random sample.
p.341: validation loss is used to pick the best model.

paragraphs.excerpt: Now, it’s time to define our model:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Opens section 11.2.2 and introduces the get_model function.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model is an encoder-decoder ConvNet: a downsampling half (Conv2D with strides) and an upsampling half (Conv2DTranspose with strides) whose output has the same height and width as the input.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Classification ConvNets end in a vector; segmentation needs one prediction per pixel, which dictates this hourglass shape.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Spatial size halves at each strided Conv2D and doubles at each strided Conv2DTranspose with padding="same": 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 → 50 → 100 → 200.

terminology.meaning: A learnable upsampling convolution, explained on p.339.
Keras layer multiplying inputs by a constant (here 1/255) inside the model.
Zero-pad so a stride-1 convolution keeps the spatial size and a stride-2 one gives exactly ceil(size/2).

connections: p.339: the model's explanation, the softmax output layer, and the Conv2D/Conv2DTranspose shape example.
p.263: strides were introduced in chapter 8.

concepts.name: Encoder-decoder segmentation ConvNet
concepts.definition: A ConvNet that first downsamples an image into compact feature maps and then upsamples them back to the input resolution to produce per-pixel outputs.
concepts.intuition: An hourglass: squeeze the image into a small, information-rich summary, then paint the answer back at full size.
concepts.technical: Encoder: Conv2D 64/64/128/128/256/256 with strides 2 on layers 1, 3, 5 → (25, 25, 256). Decoder: Conv2DTranspose 256/256/128/128/64/64 with strides 2 on layers 2, 4, 6 → (200, 200, 64), then a softmax Conv2D (p.339).
concepts.significance: The architecture used for semantic segmentation in section 11.2, summarized on p.352.
concepts.example: A 200 × 200 cat photo becomes a 25 × 25 × 256 code, then a 200 × 200 × 3 map of class probabilities.
concepts.misconception: The decoder does not simply resize pixels; its upsampling kernels are learned.

concepts.name: Strided convolution
concepts.definition: A convolution whose window moves by more than one pixel per step, downsampling the output.
concepts.intuition: Look at every other location instead of every location.
concepts.technical: With stride 2 and padding="same", output size = ceil(input/2): 200 → 100 → 50 → 25.
concepts.significance: Replaces max pooling here to keep location information (argued on p.339).
concepts.misconception: Strided convolutions are not "lossy pooling": their weights are learned.

concepts.name: Validation set
concepts.definition: Data held out from training to monitor generalization and tune choices.
concepts.intuition: A practice exam the model never studies from.
concepts.significance: Used to monitor validation loss and save the best checkpoint (p.341).
concepts.example: With about 7,390 samples, roughly 6,390 train and 1,000 validate.
concepts.misconception: Slicing the last 1,000 is only random because the data was shuffled first (p.337).

math.title: Output size of a convolution with padding="same"
math.source_text: Implied by the layer stack and the callout 'We use padding="same" everywhere to avoid the influence of border padding on feature map size.'
math.purpose: Lets you trace shapes through the model.
math.interpretation: Size depends only on the stride, not on the kernel size, which is the point of padding="same".
math.intuition: Without padding ("valid"), a 3 × 3 kernel would shave 2 pixels per layer: 200 → 198 → … and the decoder could not return to 200.

math.title: Rescaling pixel values

variables.meaning: Normalized input to the first Conv2D

math.purpose: Keep inputs in a small range for stable training (callout: 'Don't forget to rescale input images to the [0–1] range').
math.interpretation: Done inside the model, so raw images can be fed at inference time too.
math.intuition: Neural networks train best on small, roughly normalized values.

code.title: get_model: rescaling, Conv2D encoder, Conv2DTranspose decoder (continues on p.339)
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras.layers import Rescaling, Conv2D, Conv2DTranspose

def get_model(img_size, num_classes):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=img_size + (3,))
    x = Rescaling(1.0 / 255)(inputs)

    x = Conv2D(64, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(128, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(128, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(256, 3, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)
    x = Conv2D(256, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)

    x = Conv2DTranspose(256, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(256, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(128, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(128, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
code.what_it_does: Defines the first part of the segmentation model: input, rescaling, a six-layer strided Conv2D encoder down to (25, 25, 256), and a six-layer Conv2DTranspose decoder back up to (200, 200, 64). The output softmax layer, the return statement and the call get_model(img_size=img_size, num_classes=3) are on p.339.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports Keras and the three layer types used.
Callout: 'Don't forget to rescale input images to the [0–1] range.'
Encoder; callout on line 8: padding="same" everywhere avoids border effects on feature map size. Shapes: (100,100,64), (100,100,64), (50,50,128), (50,50,128), (25,25,256), (25,25,256).

code.inputs_outputs: Input: batches of (200, 200, 3) images. At this point in the code, x has shape (None, 200, 200, 64).
code.algorithm: Downsample ×8 with learned strided convolutions, then upsample ×8 with learned transposed convolutions.
code.theory_link: Hierarchical feature extraction (chapter 8) plus learned upsampling (p.339).

parameters.name: filters 64/128/256
parameters.role: Channel depth grows as resolution shrinks, the usual ConvNet pattern (p.269).

pitfalls: The decoder is not literally symmetric in placement: in the encoder the strided layer comes first in each pair; in the decoder it comes second.
Line 12 lists padding before activation; keyword order has no effect.
Input sizes not divisible by 8 would not return to the exact original size.
code.illustrative_code:
# Not from the book: inspect shapes and parameter count
model = get_model(img_size=(200, 200), num_classes=3)
model.summary()   # by our count about 2.88M parameters

deeper.title: Parameter budget of get_model
deeper.body:
Our own computation (not in the book), with 3 × 3 kernels, params = 9 · C_in · C_out + C_out:

| layer | C_in→C_out | params |
|---|---|---|
| Conv2D | 3→64 | 1,792 |
| Conv2D | 64→64 | 36,928 |
| Conv2D | 64→128 | 73,856 |
| Conv2D | 128→128 | 147,584 |
| Conv2D | 128→256 | 295,168 |
| Conv2D | 256→256 | 590,080 |
| Conv2DTranspose ×2 | 256→256 | 590,080 each |
| Conv2DTranspose | 256→128 | 295,040 |
| Conv2DTranspose | 128→128 | 147,584 |
| Conv2DTranspose | 128→64 | 73,792 |
| Conv2DTranspose | 64→64 | 36,928 |
| Conv2D softmax (p.339) | 64→3 | 1,731 |

Total ≈ **2,880,643** parameters. Most of them sit in the 256-channel layers at the bottleneck.

deeper.title: Why rescale inside the model
deeper.body: Beyond the book: you could divide the NumPy arrays by 255 beforehand, but putting `Rescaling` in the model means the saved model accepts raw 0–255 images directly, so preprocessing cannot be forgotten or done inconsistently at inference (p.341 feeds a raw test image).

visualizations.why: 1,000 of roughly 7,390 samples are held out for validation (about 13.5%), with no separate test set in this example.

misconceptions.claim: padding="same" means the output always has the same size as the input.
misconceptions.correction: Only for stride 1. With stride 2 it gives exactly half (Conv2D) or double (Conv2DTranspose); 'same' removes the border shrinkage, not the stride effect.

misconceptions.claim: The targets need to be one-hot encoded with 3 channels.
misconceptions.correction: They are integer labels in one channel; sparse categorical cross-entropy (p.340) handles them directly.

misconceptions.claim: The decoder halves the number of filters because it needs fewer parameters.
misconceptions.correction: It mirrors the encoder: as resolution rises, depth falls, keeping computation per layer balanced. (Interpretation, not stated in the book.)

earlier.note: The pattern of increasing depth and decreasing feature-map size in ConvNets.

later.note: Output softmax layer, why strides beat max pooling here, and how Conv2DTranspose upsamples.

related_code.note: First half of the loading code block.

takeaways: Inputs: float32 (N, 200, 200, 3); targets: uint8 (N, 200, 200, 1) with labels 0–2.
The last 1,000 shuffled samples form the validation set.
Rescaling(1/255) inside the model normalizes pixels.
Encoder: Conv2D with stride 2 every other layer, 200 → 25; decoder: Conv2DTranspose with stride 2 every other layer, 25 → 200.
padding="same" everywhere makes feature-map sizes depend only on strides.

questions.question: What is the shape of x right after the six Conv2D layers?
questions.explanation: Three stride-2 layers halve 200 three times: 100, 50, 25; the last layers have 256 filters. (100,100,64) and (50,50,128) are intermediate shapes; 12 would need a fourth stride.

questions.question: Why is the targets array uint8 with one channel while input_imgs is float32 with three?
questions.answer: Targets hold one integer class label per pixel; inputs hold RGB values that will be processed as floats.
questions.explanation: From the callout on the loading loop.

questions.question: Without padding="same" (i.e. with 'valid' padding and stride 1), what would a 3 × 3 Conv2D do to a 100 × 100 feature map, and why is that a problem here?
questions.answer: It would produce 98 × 98; the shrinkage accumulates, so the decoder would not end exactly at 200 × 200 to match the masks.
questions.explanation: Valid output size = H − k + 1 = 100 − 3 + 1 = 98. The callout says padding='same' avoids border effects on feature-map size.

questions.question: What does input_imgs[:-num_val_samples] select?
questions.answer: All samples except the last 1,000, which become the training inputs.
questions.explanation: Negative slicing; the complementary slice [-1000:] is the validation set.

questions.question: Why must the model's final spatial size equal the input's?
questions.answer: Because the loss compares a prediction for every pixel with the 200 × 200 mask; the output must provide one class distribution per mask pixel.
questions.explanation: That is the motivation for the Conv2DTranspose decoder explained on p.339.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Rescaling(1.0 / 255)?
options: Normalize each image to zero mean
questions.explanation: The callout says rescale input images to the [0–1] range. Resizing was done by load_img, labels are untouched, and no mean subtraction is performed.

questions.question: Can you write down the shape after each of the 12 hidden layers without looking?
questions.explanation: Halve at each strided Conv2D, double at each strided Conv2DTranspose; channels = filters.
